newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals--Cobalt, antimony seen probing higher.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals--Cobalt, antimony seen probing higher.

text.p: Cobalt and antimony prices appear to have bottomed out and are set to probe higher, although molybdenum has eased and magnesium is mostly stagnant, strategic metal traders in Asia said on Tuesday.
Cobalt prices are inching upward amid solid demand from Japanese end users, as sentiment grows that the market has found a floor after recent declines.

Traders were eyeing the continued advance of Zairean rebels in that country's cobalt-rich Shaba Province as well as results due on Friday of bidding for low-grade cobalt from the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency stockpile.
"Nothing has changed in the fundamentals ... but cobalt had been falling for a long time and there was a feeling it had reached fair value," said one source at a large trade house.
Another trader added, "There's a consensus that the market has a firmer tone," although he said supplies were not tight.
Traders had divergent views on current prices, however. One said buyers would have to pay $22 a lb or more for high-grade metal while another said prices were still below $21.
In the antimony market, Chinese sources said languishing prices could start a rebound in the foreseeable future, having hit bottom on little activity.
The head of a major trading house in Hong Kong with connections to the government of Hunan province said he expected to see some strengthening of prices as industrial demand for the metal improved.
A non-ferrous metals conference in Hong Kong heard from a Chinese metals industry official on Tuesday that China had drawn down much of its antimony stockpile and would reduce output in 1997.

Zheng Fengren, director of Hsikwangshan Mining Administration, said current world antimony prices of around $2,200 a tonne were not high enough to sustain Chinese production and had forced many factories to close down.
Chinese antimony was now being offered at $2,300 a tonne, compared to between $2,400 to $2,500 in January, he said.
Traders said Chinese antimony ingots were being offered at $2,250 a tonne inclusive of cost and freight (C&F) in Rotterdam late last month.
But with little interest in buying at that level, the Chinese could easily be beaten down to $2,200 a tonne, one source in Hong Kong said.

Official Chinese customs figures showed the country's exports of unwrought antimony reached 2,035 tonnes in January, up 10.5 percent from the year-ago period, while total exports in 1996 rose 22.5 percent to 31,192 tonnes.
Tungsten trade was slow, with wolframite ore still difficult to source, traders said.
Molybdenum demand remained healthy, trade sources said, but prices retraced a bit after rallying early in the year.
One Hong Kong source said Chinese producers were having no trouble moving their material.
"Even the producers don't want the price to go too high because this discourages buying and could see users recycling or substituting," he said.
The magnesium market was steady, a Japanese trade house source said, supported by relatively low levels of consumer stocks although supplies were sufficient to meet demand.
